last_transition_reason: The proof is mathematically sound and complete for the stated lemma. It correctly rewrites q-binomial coefficients via P_m(q), uses the symmetry [n choose r]_q = [n choose n-r]_q to reduce to a = min(k,n-k) and b = min(l,n-l), and then proves by contradiction that a < b is impossible if the quotient is polynomial. The root-of-unity argument is valid: under a < b one has b < n-a, so a primitive (n-a)-th root of unity annihilates the denominator product B(q) but not the numerator product A(q), contradicting polynomiality after cross-multiplication. This matches the lemma sketch and the role in the assembly, and no forbidden or undeclared theorem citations are used.
latest_nl_proof:
Let P_m(q) := product_{j=1}^m (1 - q^j) for m >= 0, with P_0(q) = 1.

For any r with 0 <= r <= n, the given definition gives
[n choose r]_q = (product_{i=1}^r (1 - q^(n-r+i))) / (product_{i=1}^r (1 - q^i)).
Reindexing the numerator product,
product_{i=1}^r (1 - q^(n-r+i)) = product_{j=n-r+1}^n (1 - q^j) = P_n(q)/P_{n-r}(q).
Hence
[n choose r]_q = P_n(q) / (P_r(q) P_{n-r}(q)).
Therefore, for every r,
[n choose r]_q = [n choose n-r]_q
as rational functions.

Now set a := k0 = min(k, n-k) and b := l0 = min(l, n-l). Since a is either k or n-k, the symmetry above shows [n choose k]_q = [n choose a]_q. Similarly, [n choose l]_q = [n choose b]_q. So the hypothesis implies that
F(q) := [n choose a]_q / [n choose b]_q
is a polynomial in q.

We prove a >= b. Assume for contradiction that a < b.
Because a = min(k, n-k) and b = min(l, n-l), we have a <= n/2 and b <= n/2. Since a < b, we have a <= b-1, so
n - a >= n - b + 1.
Also b <= n/2 implies n - b >= b, hence n - b + 1 > b. Therefore
n - a > b.

Using the formula [n choose r]_q = P_n/(P_r P_{n-r}), we compute
F(q) = (P_b(q) P_{n-b}(q)) / (P_a(q) P_{n-a}(q))
     = (product_{i=a+1}^b (1 - q^i)) / (product_{i=n-b+1}^{n-a} (1 - q^i)).
Write
A(q) := product_{i=a+1}^b (1 - q^i),
B(q) := product_{i=n-b+1}^{n-a} (1 - q^i),
so that F(q) = A(q)/B(q).

Now choose a complex primitive (n-a)-th root of unity zeta.
Because every exponent i occurring in A satisfies 1 <= i <= b < n-a, we have zeta^i != 1 for all such i. Hence A(zeta) != 0.

For B, the factor with i = n-a is 1 - zeta^(n-a) = 0. Every other exponent i in B satisfies 1 <= i < n-a, so zeta^i != 1 for those i. Thus B(zeta) = 0.

If F(q) were a polynomial, say F(q) = R(q) with R in C[q], then A(q) = R(q) B(q) in C[q]. Evaluating at q = zeta would give
A(zeta) = R(zeta) B(zeta) = 0,
contradicting A(zeta) != 0.

So F(q) cannot be a polynomial. This contradicts the hypothesis. Therefore our assumption a < b was false, and we must have a >= b.

Since a = k0 and b = l0, this is exactly k0 >= l0.
role_in_parent: Shows that after complement reduction the numerator index is at least the denominator index, so the shifted-interval product has nonnegative length.
statement_nl: For integers n, k, and l with 0 <= k <= n and 0 <= l <= n, define [n choose r]_q := product_{i=1}^r (1 - q^(n-r+i)) / (1 - q^i) for 0 <= r <= n, with the empty product equal to 1 when r = 0. Let k0 := min(k, n-k) and l0 := min(l, n-l). If the rational function [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q is actually a polynomial in q, then k0 >= l0.

domain_restrictions: n, k, and l are integers.
k and l satisfy 0 <= k <= n and 0 <= l <= n.
The q-binomial coefficient is only defined by the given product for integers r in the range 0 <= r <= n.
The empty product is interpreted as 1 when r = 0.
The quotient [n choose k]_q divided by [n choose l]_q is considered as a rational function in q.
The hypothesis requires that this rational function actually belongs to the polynomial ring in q, not merely that it is formally written as a quotient.
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every choice of integers n, k, and l with 0 <= k <= n and 0 <= l <= n, if the ratio of the two q-binomial coefficients [n choose k]_q and [n choose l]_q is a polynomial in q, then min(k, n-k) is at least min(l, n-l).
quantifier_order: For all integers n, k, and l, assume 0 <= k <= n and 0 <= l <= n.
For each integer r with 0 <= r <= n, define the q-binomial coefficient using the stated product, with the empty product equal to 1 when r = 0.
Define k0 as the minimum of k and n-k, and define l0 as the minimum of l and n-l.
If the quotient of the two q-binomial coefficients is a polynomial in q, then the conclusion follows.
